attribution.note: Marcus says in his own voice that LLMs still have a truthiness problem. He is restating his own earlier warning, not quoting anyone else.

semantics.note: The 'and they have' part is a present-tense observation that the problem persisted. Rendering 'truthiness' as 'truthfulness' is a fair paraphrase.

contract.note: Reading 'truthiness' as confident factual errors in widely used LLMs during 2024–2026 is ordinary and fair. The contract does not require error rates to stay flat or rise, so improvement alone does not count against the claim.

evidence.note: OpenAI disclosure dated Sep 2025, before the post. It concedes that GPT-5's hallucinations still occur and gives examples of confident wrong answers. It is a company disclosure, but it admits a problem, and it meets the contract's 'documented outputs' standard.

reviews.rationale: A dated 2025 disclosure from a leading developer admits that its flagship model still makes plausible-sounding false statements and calls hallucination a basic problem for all LLMs. The improvement it reports does not contradict persistence under the contract. Nothing in the packet shows fabrication had stopped being a material problem.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion, in his own essay.

semantics.note: Both parts of the conjunction are kept: late, and short of expectations. The normalised text leaves out the emphatic 'by any reasonable measure', but the contract addresses it.

contract.note: Marcus named no measure. Reading 'late' against OpenAI's own earlier plans and 'short' as a substantial gap against publicly anticipated capability is ordinary and fair. Because no expectation baseline is defined, the result depends on that interpretation.

evidence.note: Contemporary April 2025 report that GPT-5 would come later than originally anticipated. This supports the 'late' part.
Release announcement dated Aug 7, 2025, which fixes the release date. Its performance claims are the company's own and not independent.

Documents months of hype, one expert calling the launch underwhelming, and user frustration. The same article also reports mixed reviews and a router fault, so it only weakly supports a broad shortfall.
A favourable firsthand review from a preview tester cuts against sweeping disappointment. It does not show that pre-release expectations were met.

reviews.rationale: The 'late' part holds: OpenAI pushed GPT-5 back and released it in August 2025. The 'short of expectations' part is not established, because the packet shows only mixed early reception, gives no defined pre-release capability baseline, and includes favourable assessments. One part of the conjunction is supported and the other is unsettled, so the claim as a whole is unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own causal assertion, in his own essay.

semantics.note: Read as a causal claim that DeepSeek's competition caused OpenAI's dramatic price cuts. Treating 'Altman' as standing for OpenAI is reasonable.

contract.note: Reading 'forced' as 'materially caused, not necessarily the only cause' and limiting the claim to API list prices is ordinary and fair. Marcus named no product or comparison period, so the reading matters to the result.

evidence.note: OpenAI announced an 80% o3 API cut in June 2025, a substantial reduction. Nothing in the item ties it to DeepSeek.

June 2025 report that OpenAI credited inference optimisation for the cut. That is a competing explanation, not proof that competition played no part. The sidebar links are later page clutter and were not used.
Jan 2025 report expecting DeepSeek's price war to reach the US. It is a forecast and does not show what caused any OpenAI pricing decision.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows a dramatic OpenAI price cut and earlier predictions of DeepSeek-driven pricing pressure. But no direct evidence connects the cut to DeepSeek, and OpenAI attributed it to efficiency gains. The packet neither establishes the causal link nor rules it out.
